newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China slams HK subversion law, quizzes candidates.
newsitem.headline: China slams HK subversion law, quizzes candidates.

text.p: China pressed ahead with plans to shape post-colonial Hong Kong on Wednesday, lashing out at a proposal for a soft law on subversion and quizzing potential leaders of the territory after it reverts to Beijing's control.

"Britain violated its promise that all major issues must be decided through negotiations with China in the latter stage of transition," a spokesman from China's de facto embassy in the territory said.

The row over the proposed law was sparked on Tuesday when the Hong Kong government said it would gazette a bill defining treason, sedition, subversion and secession as a way to head off Chinese-style jailings of dissidents after Beijing takes over the colony at midnight next June 30.
A senior negotiator on the handover, Chen Zuo'er, said Britain should not have acted unilaterally but declined to say whether China would repeal the bill if it became law.
Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten, speaking in Tokyo, defended his government's move to introduce the bill and criticised Beijing for refusing to talk about the issue.
"We've been discussing for 17 months -- 17 months -- with Chinese officials on this issue and frankly, by and large, Chinese officials have refused to enter into a dialogue," he said.

The proposed law did nothing to contravene the Joint Declaration between Britain and China, he said, adding that a breach of the pact came from China, which plans to scrap Hong Kong's elected legislature in favour of a provisional body.
"People living in glass houses should be careful of lobbing bricks around," Patten said.
The three candidates vying to lead Hong Kong after the handover faced the 400-member China-controlled Selection Committee on Wednesday to answer questions on their platforms.
Billionaire shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa warned that if Asian-style "money politics" existed in the territory, it would be the end of Hong Kong.

Businessman Peter Woo said he "regretted" that the government had proposed a new anti-subversion law without China's consent, adding that few changes should be made to the territory's laws in the run-up to handover.
Yang Ti Liang, a former chief justice, said the provisional legislature, to be formed on December 21, should meet outside the territory before the handover.
"We don't want to see that the first lawsuit filed in Hong Kong court after the handover is on the legality of the provisional legislature," he said.
Democratic Party leader Martin Lee has said he would lodge an injunction to prevent the operation of the provisional legislature in parallel with the current Legislative Council.
Selection Committee members, who are charged with choosing the territory's post-colonial leader on December 11, said Tung's platform was the most comprehensive.

"All three are good," Selection Committee member Chan Wing-kee told reporters after the meeting. "But I feel Tung is the best. He raises the problems faced by Hong Kong and comes up with solutions to them in his platform."

Hong Kong's stock market seemed unfazed by any of the developments, rising to its 16th record high of the year. The Hang Seng Index put on 45.62 points to 13,530.95 on huge turnover of $13.42 billion.

U.S. senators John Glenn and Thomas Daschle, who recently returned to Washington after a trip to Hong Kong and other Asian countries, said on Monday they were optimistic about Hong Kong's peaceful transition to Chinese rule.

"China insists that it's going to be peaceful, insists that it's going to continue with the same system there, and we all hope that is right, of course," Glenn said. "I personally am optimistic about that one because I think it's to China's advantage."
